canonical_question: Does the 'strongest damping peak' in N-2 HEA result from the sum of the two high-temperature peaks (0.027 and 0.009) alone, or does the low-temperature peak (0.002) play a negligible role?

question_variants.question: Does the 'strongest damping peak' in N-2 HEA result from the sum of the two high-temperature peaks (0.027 and 0.009) alone, or does the low-temperature peak (0.002) play a negligible role?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The strongest damping peak in N-2 HEA is indeed the sum of the three peaks: the low-temperature peak (0.002) and the two high-temperature peaks (0.027 and 0.009). The low-temperature peak is not negligible; it contributes to the total, though the high-temperature peaks dominate the magnitude.

answers.answer: The N-2 HEA shows three peaks with heights of 0.002 (low-temperature), 0.027, and 0.009 (high-temperature). The paper states the N-2 HEA has the strongest damping peak among all three HEAs studied, which results from the combination of these peaks.
answers.mechanism: Ordered nitrogen complexes cause the low-temperature peak; random atoms cause high-temperature peaks.
evidence_spans: For the nitrogen-doped N-2 HEA, an additional low-temperature peak (blue curve) and two high-temperature peaks (green and magenta curves) were also observed (see Fig. 5C ).
The peak height of the additional low-temperature peak is 0.002, and that of the two high-temperature peaks is 0.027 and 0.009, respectively.
Hence, only ~5.3% of all the nitrogen atoms in the N-2 HEA contribute to the formation of ordered nitrogen complexes.
